claims.text: The baseline alloy is equiatomic NbMoTaW.
Equiatomic NbMoTaW has excellent high-temperature mechanical performance up to 1600 °C.
Equiatomic NbMoTaW has poor room-temperature ductility.
Experimental irradiation data for NbMoTaW are limited, and its irradiation resistance has mainly been inferred computationally.
Adding approximately 5 at% V to NbMoTaW increases local lattice distortion.
V-induced lattice distortion lowers the critical stress for nanotwin nucleation in NbMoTaW.
V addition combined with warm rolling and annealing will produce coherent, high-density nanotwin boundaries and/or fine twin-like precipitates in the BCC matrix.
The proposed nanotwin structures provide additional room-temperature plastic-deformation mechanisms.
The modified alloy will exhibit a potentially greater than 50% increase in room-temperature ductility relative to untreated NbMoTaW.
High-density twin boundaries act as sinks for irradiation-induced point defects and helium bubbles.
The modified alloy will have lower irradiation-induced defect density than untreated NbMoTaW.
The modified alloy will exhibit reduced helium-bubble connectivity relative to untreated NbMoTaW.
The proposed twin-boundary mechanism will mitigate irradiation-induced amorphization.
The proposed twin-boundary mechanism will mitigate helium-induced blistering.
The approximately 5 at% V modification will preserve single-phase BCC stability.
The approximately 5 at% V modification will preserve NbMoTaW high-temperature strength up to 1600 °C.
The predicted irradiation benefit applies under helium implantation up to approximately 1 dpa and temperatures up to 800 °C.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis promises single-phase BCC stability while also proposing fine-scale precipitates. If those precipitates constitute a distinct phase, their formation is inconsistent with a strictly single-phase alloy; the text does not clarify whether 'twin-like precipitates' are merely structural domains or a secondary phase.
